The authors reported the first experimental realization of birefringent transformation optics (TO) devices.

The devices were based on lithographically defined metal/dielectric waveguides, where adiabatic variations of the waveguide shape enabled control of the effective refractive indices for TE and TM modes.
One device operated as a Luneburg lens for TM polarized light, while behaving as a spatial (directional) filter for TE polarized light.
Another device functioned as a Luneburg lens for TM light, while exhibiting an approximate semi-classical cloaking Hamiltonian for TE polarized light.
The Luneburg lens devices achieved almost diffraction-limited (~0.7λ) focusing of 515 nm light, which is an order of magnitude improvement over previous TO lens fabrication.
The devices demonstrated broadband performance, with similar focusing behavior observed at 515 nm and 633 nm.
The authors used a lithography technique to precisely control the thickness profile d(r) of the dielectric photoresist layer, enabling control of the effective refractive indices.

Variations of the waveguide thickness in the 0.1-0.3 μm range allowed obtaining very strong variations of the TE effective refractive index in the 0<neff<1.4 range, while keeping the TM refractive index approximately constant at neff>1.3.
The effective refractive index for TE waves was imaginary only within an extremely thin, 20 nm rim at the edge of the device, allowing significant TE light transmission.
The authors used a near-field scanning optical microscope (NSOM) to characterize the optical field distributions in the fabricated devices.
The work opens up an additional degree of freedom in optical design and improves the ability to manipulate light on the submicrometer scale using birefringent transformation optics devices.
The authors demonstrated the first experimental realization of birefringent TO devices that perform different functions for orthogonal polarization states of light.
The devices were fabricated using lithographically defined metal/dielectric waveguides with adiabatic variations in the waveguide shape.
The Luneburg lens devices achieved almost diffraction-limited focusing, an order of magnitude improvement over previous TO lens fabrication.
The devices demonstrated broadband performance and polarization-dependent behavior, which was characterized using an NSOM.
